book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Why these five papers?
episodes.subtitle: The evidence pipeline behind an AI answer

scenes.title: An answer appears
scenes.claim: Before checking the answer, ask: why these papers?
scenes.narration: You ask an academic AI assistant: is there an open access citation advantage? An answer appears, with five papers and neat little citation numbers. The papers are real. The summary sounds convincing. But before checking what the answer says, ask a different question. Why these five papers?

scenes.title: Two machines, one product
scenes.claim: Retrieval selects and orders records; generation writes from supplied evidence
scenes.narration: Imagine two machines. Retrieval selects and orders records. Generation turns some of those records into prose. We usually stare at the second machine. Chapter one asks us to look inside the first.

scenes.title: Follow the evidence
scenes.claim: Documented pipeline: Boolean conversion → up to 30 candidates → 5 sources → overview
scenes.narration: Here is the Primo Research Assistant pipeline documented in the chapter. A language model rewrites the question into Boolean variations connected by OR. That query searches the Central Discovery Index. Up to thirty results enter the candidate set. An embedding based reranking step selects five sources. Only then does a language model write an overview from their abstracts. A language model helped write the query, too. So hearing that a product uses an LLM does not tell you how it retrieves.

scenes.title: The shortlist bottleneck
scenes.claim: A fixed candidate pool cannot recover a paper that never entered it
scenes.narration: Let's turn that into a picture. Each dot is a record in the index. Retrieval moves a small candidate set through the first boundary. Reranking changes their order. Selection keeps five. The writer receives only this smaller working set. Now notice the gold dot. It is a relevant paper, but it never entered the candidate set. Reordering that set cannot bring it back. Within this retrieval round, supplied evidence can shrink. Fluent writing cannot establish source supported coverage of a paper that was never supplied. This is the shortlist bottleneck. Another retrieval round could add evidence. A prettier answer cannot.

scenes.title: Where did the paper go?
scenes.claim: A missing citation alone does not identify where the paper was lost
scenes.narration: But a missing citation is not a diagnosis. The paper might be outside the index, missed by the query, or cut off at a candidate boundary. It might enter the thirty candidates and lose its place when five are selected. Or it might reach the writer and still be omitted. Inspect the working set before blaming a machine. Retrieval limits the supplied evidence. It does not guarantee that every generated claim uses that evidence.

scenes.title: A map of the machinery
scenes.claim: Six possible stages; a controller chooses and sequences actions
scenes.narration: Zoom out. A useful map has six possible stages: query transformation, analysis and execution rules, first stage retrieval, fusion, reranking, and presentation. Fusion combines candidate lists, perhaps from different queries or retrieval methods. Not every product uses every stage. A controller chooses and sequences the actions. The shape of an answer does not reveal who chose the next search.

scenes.title: Two independent axes
scenes.claim: Output and retrieval iteration are independent; agency is a separate question
scenes.narration: Separate two properties. Across this axis, the output changes from ranked records to a written answer. Up this axis, retrieval changes from a single pass to repeated searches. That gives us quick search, quick answer, iterative search, and deep research. Neither axis measures agency. A fixed workflow and an agent can occupy the same box.

episodes.title: A match is not relevance
episodes.subtitle: One study, two purposes, different contributions

scenes.title: The query is a representation
scenes.claim: Queries, filters and task briefs can express substantial detail about the need
scenes.narration: A carefully built search makes its conditions explicit and inspectable. A record that passes them has passed a useful test. But does it help with the task? Behind the search is an information need: what a person wants to know or accomplish. Queries, filters, and task briefs can express substantial detail about it. The query represents the need. It is not the need itself.

scenes.title: From a need to a judgement
scenes.claim: Detailed requests and feedback help the system estimate suitability
scenes.narration: Follow the chain: information need, query or representation, retrieval signals, retrieved or ranked records, then human judgement. The system works directly with the middle three. A detailed request can communicate the purpose. Feedback can communicate judgements. The system can use both to estimate suitability; the reader still assesses whether a record helps.

scenes.title: A skilled search expresses more
scenes.claim: Alternative terminology and a date limit communicate a detailed need
scenes.narration: Take the chapter's hypothetical search: recent empirical studies of generative AI services for research support in academic libraries. The librarian combines alternative terms: generative AI or large language models; academic library or university library; research support or research consultation. Publications must be from twenty twenty four onwards. This strategy expresses much more of the need than a few broad keywords.

scenes.title: The study passes the search
scenes.claim: The hypothetical demonstration study meets the conditions and is topically suitable
scenes.narration: The search retrieves an empirical study of a university library's generative AI research support service. Participants report positive reactions after a short demonstration. It meets the search conditions and is topically suitable. Now keep that same paper in view while we change the purpose.

scenes.title: Same paper, different purpose
scenes.claim: The contribution changes with the task; the search match stays the same
scenes.narration: For a workshop introducing possible applications, the study offers a useful example of a service and how participants responded. For a decision about introducing the service, it contributes less. Positive reactions after a demonstration offer limited evidence about answer accuracy, staff workload, or performance in actual research consultations. The paper is not wholly irrelevant to that decision. It just does not establish what the decision maker needs to know. Its search match has not changed.

scenes.title: Search better, then assess the evidence
scenes.claim: Better searching and relevance judgement work together; a score remains an estimate
scenes.narration: Refine the search to seek accuracy evaluations or operational evidence. Then assess the resulting studies: what did they measure, under what conditions, and how well does that evidence support the decision? Better searching and relevance judgement work together. When Primo Research Assistant selects five sources, its score is an estimate based on available evidence and training. A high score for the demonstration study cannot turn participant reactions into evidence of answer accuracy.

scenes.title: Relevant to whom, for what?
scenes.claim: Relevance is a relationship: to someone, for something
scenes.narration: Relevant can mean a computed match, topical suitability, what a person learns, or usefulness for a task. These are related perspectives, not a fixed ladder. A model can estimate topical or task specific suitability. That estimate is still different from the reader's experienced usefulness. Relevance is a relationship: relevant to someone, for something. A match is evidence, not the judgement.

episodes.title: Three clues hiding in a search box
episodes.subtitle: What visible results can and cannot tell us

scenes.title: Puzzle 1: the impossible word
scenes.claim: Returned papers challenge a strict-AND assumption; they do not establish an architecture
scenes.narration: Chapter one leaves us with three puzzles. First, add an invented word to a real question. If strict AND requires that word, the result set should be empty. Yet the chapter's scite example still returns useful looking papers. Does that prove semantic retrieval? No. It challenges our assumption about the admission rule. Keep the internal mechanism open. A screen shows behaviour, not a complete architecture.

scenes.title: Puzzle 2: the invisible results
scenes.claim: A reported count is not evidence that every record was scored or ranked
scenes.narration: Second, the chapter's Google Scholar search reports about nine point four million results, while only a thousand are viewable. Animate those quantities separately. The reported count is enormous. The visible window is tiny. The count alone does not tell us that every record was individually scored or ranked. How was the viewable fraction chosen?

scenes.title: Puzzle 3: the shrinking question
scenes.claim: A product name does not establish its retrieval architecture
scenes.narration: Third, in the chapter's August twenty twenty six Semantic Scholar observation, the full question returns thirteen results. Remove the extra question words, and the shorter keyword query returns about thirty five thousand three hundred. Same need. Very different result counts. A name containing semantic does not establish a retrieval architecture. These observations are prompts to investigate, not proof of a hidden mechanism.

scenes.title: Inspect the working set
scenes.claim: First inspect whether the missing paper entered the working set
scenes.narration: Try this. Five real, accurately summarised papers appear, but the landmark paper is missing. Which machine failed? First ask whether it entered the working set. If it did, inspect selection and generation. If it did not, trace the query, index, candidate boundary, and reranking. Finding it with a new direct search tests availability. It does not prove where the original run lost it.

scenes.title: Follow the evidence backwards
scenes.claim: What was supplied? What was selected? What was searched?
scenes.narration: So when an answer arrives, follow the evidence backwards. What was supplied? What was selected? What was searched? That is the retrieval problem. Chapter two begins with the clearest admission rule of all: words as Boolean conditions.
